anchorData: FIRST 20 ELEMENTS (symbol, name, atomic number Z, relative atomic mass A_r rounded, electron arrangement in s and p notation, group, period). H hydrogen Z1 A_r 1 1s1 group 1 period 1. He helium Z2 A_r 4 1s2 group 18 period 1. Li lithium Z3 A_r 7 1s2 2s1 group 1 period 2. Be beryllium Z4 A_r 9 1s2 2s2 group 2 period 2. B boron Z5 A_r 11 1s2 2s2 2p1 group 13 period 2. C carbon Z6 A_r 12 1s2 2s2 2p2 group 14 period 2. N nitrogen Z7 A_r 14 1s2 2s2 2p3 group 15 period 2. O oxygen Z8 A_r 16 1s2 2s2 2p4 group 16 period 2. F fluorine Z9 A_r 19 1s2 2s2 2p5 group 17 period 2. Ne neon Z10 A_r 20 1s2 2s2 2p6 group 18 period 2. Na sodium Z11 A_r 23 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 group 1 period 3. Mg magnesium Z12 A_r 24 ...3s2 group 2 period 3. Al aluminium Z13 A_r 27 ...3s2 3p1 group 13 period 3. Si silicon Z14 A_r 28 ...3s2 3p2 group 14 period 3. P phosphorus Z15 A_r 31 ...3s2 3p3 group 15 period 3. S sulfur Z16 A_r 32 ...3s2 3p4 group 16 period 3. Cl chlorine Z17 A_r 35.5 ...3s2 3p5 group 17 period 3. Ar argon Z18 A_r 40 ...3s2 3p6 group 18 period 3. K potassium Z19 A_r 39 ...3s2 3p6 4s1 group 1 period 4. Ca calcium Z20 A_r 40 ...3s2 3p6 4s2 group 2 period 4. (Full notation for Na onward starts with 1s2 2s2 2p6.) Group number for main groups: group 1, 2 = number of outer electrons; group 13-18 = outer electrons + 10 (so 13 to 18 have 3 to 8 outer electrons; He has 2). Period number = number of occupied energy levels. Key comparisons: Li 7, Na 23, K 39 are very different in mass but each has 1 outer electron and all react vigorously with water; reactivity increases down the group Li < Na < K. Ne (Z10) and Ar (Z18) have full outer levels (8 outer electrons) and do not react; He has a full 1s2 (duplet). Mass anomaly: Ar A_r 40 is larger than K A_r 39 though Ar Z18 comes before K Z19, which shows order is by atomic number not mass (Moseley). Ca A_r 40 equals Ar A_r 40 but they are in different groups. Ion data: Li+ Na+ K+ (group 1, charge 1+); Be2+ Mg2+ Ca2+ (2+); Al3+ (3+); N3- O2- F- (3-, 2-, 1-); P3- S2- Cl- (3-, 2-, 1-). Na+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 (same as Ne); Cl- is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (same as Ar); K+ and Ca2+ are same as Ar; Mg2+ and O2- and F- same as Ne. Oxidation numbers: Na +1, Mg +2, Al +3, Cl -1, O -2. Variable oxidation numbers: iron Fe2+ (+2) and Fe3+ (+3); copper Cu+ (+1) and Cu2+ (+2) (transition elements; not predicted by outer-electron count alone). Radicals (charge): nitrate NO3- , hydroxide OH-, sulfate SO4 2-, carbonate CO3 2-, ammonium NH4+, phosphate PO4 3-. Formulae: NaCl, MgO, CaCl2, Al2O3, KNO3 (potassium nitrate fertilizer), K2SO4, Ca(NO3)2, (NH4)2SO4 (ammonium sulfate fertilizer), NaOH, Fe2O3, FeCl2, CuO. Equations: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 ; 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2 ; 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2 ; 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl ; 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 ; Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2. Reaction with water observation (qualitative): Li fizzes steadily and floats; Na melts into a ball and darts, fizzes fast; K melts, burns with lilac flame, very vigorous. Water treatment: chlorine (Cl2) used to disinfect water in Nairobi and Mombasa; fluoride compounds also present in some water supplies. Historical: Mendeleev 1869 arranged by atomic mass and left gaps predicting undiscovered elements; Moseley 1913 showed atomic number is the true basis of order; the modern table uses atomic number.
characters: Learners: Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina, Kipchoge (Grade 10 class at a school in Kisumu, shared by all lessons, used as names in examples only). Teacher: Mwalimu Achieng. Mendeleev (Russian chemist, 1869, ordered by mass and left gaps). Moseley (English physicist, 1913, atomic number). Element cards: set of 20 cards showing symbol, atomic number, A_r and properties but NOT position, used from lesson 1 to sort. Driving Question Board (DQB): class wall chart started in lesson 1. Class Model: a poster 'Electron Arrangement Model' revised each lesson. Places: Nairobi and Mombasa (chlorine water treatment), Kericho and Rift Valley (farms using potassium fertilizers such as KNO3, and ammonium sulfate), Lake Victoria (water source treated with chlorine). Unfamiliar element for lesson 10 prediction: strontium (Sr, Z38, group 2) or gallium; use strontium (Z38, outer electrons 2, forms Sr2+, formula SrCl2, SrO) with its electron arrangement given as 2,8,18,8,2 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6 5s2.
outcome: Elements are ordered by atomic number, and the number of outer-shell electrons decides the group while the number of occupied energy levels decides the period. Elements in the same group (Li, Na, K) have the same outer electron count so they react alike despite very different masses, while neighbours (Na, Mg, Ne, Ar) differ because their outer electron counts differ. Atoms lose, gain or (in lesson 10 link to bonding) share electrons to reach the stable noble gas arrangement, which explains why Ne and Ar are unreactive, why group 1 metals form 1+ ions, why chlorine forms Cl-, and lets us predict ions, valencies and formulae such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3 and KNO3 for any element.
conventions: Use 'electron arrangement' with both forms: energy-level form (e.g. 2,8,1) and s and p notation (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1); the s and p notation is used from lesson 3 onward and both are shown together. Outer electrons = valence electrons. Group numbers 1 to 18 (IUPAC); also say 'group 1 (I)' only where needed. Period = number of occupied energy levels. Atomic number Z = protons = electrons in neutral atom; mass number A = protons + neutrons; use A_r for relative atomic mass. Cation = positive ion (loses electrons); anion = negative ion (gains electrons). Write ion charges as superscripts in text like Na+ , Mg2+, O2-, with the number before the sign. Valency = number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares (always positive whole number); oxidation number has sign (+1, -2) and is written with sign before the number. Dot-and-cross diagrams: dots for electrons of one atom, crosses for the other. Radicals are charged groups of atoms that stay together (NO3-, SO4 2-, OH-, NH4+, CO3 2-). Formulae: criss-cross method of valencies, brackets around radicals when subscript needed, e.g. Ca(NO3)2. Equations include state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) from lesson 9; balance by adjusting coefficients only, never subscripts. Use 'noble gases' (not inert gases). Use the DQB, Class Model, and Element Cards names consistently. Lesson 4 families: alkali metals (group 1), alkaline earth metals (group 2), halogens (group 17), noble gases (group 18), transition elements (between group 2 and 13 in the periods 4 and beyond). Do not teach bond types in detail; lesson 10 only previews the octet rule and that bonding (sub-strand 1.4) explains how atoms share electrons.
